# Exact mixed Stein identity and a signed flux at an active deepest cap

This note gives an integration-by-parts identity for a finite union of
integer fibers. It also constructs a convex mixed-integer body for which
the integer flux is strictly negative at an actual globally deepest point
and an actual minimizing cap, even though the cap section has that point
as its full ambient centroid. It does not prove the mixed-integer
Grunbaum conjecture or an inequality below its target constant.

## 1. Finite-measure formulation, including closed-cap atoms

Let `P` be a finite nonempty set of integer indices. At each `z in P` let `mu_z`
be a nonzero finite positive measure on a compact continuous fiber. Put

    w_z = mu_z(R^d),   M = sum_z w_z,
    L(z,x) = v.z + u.x,
    nu_z = L_# mu_z,
    m_z = (1/w_z) integral s dnu_z(s),
    m = (1/M) sum_z w_z m_z.

No density assumption is needed. In particular this applies to the
positive-measure fibers of intrinsic Hausdorff measure `H_q` in the task;
zero-measure fibers are omitted from `P`. Define the CLOSED tail quantities

    P_z(t) = nu_z([t,infinity))/w_z,
    kappa_z(t) = integral_[t,infinity) (s-m_z) dnu_z(s).

For every real `t`, `kappa_z(t)>=0`. When `t>=m_z` this is immediate.
When `t<m_z`, the integral equals the negative of the centered integral
over `(-infinity,t)`, whose integrand is negative. This argument includes
atoms at `t` without replacing a closed cap by an open one.

Choose any oriented spanning tree on `P`, and choose an edge flow `F_e`
whose incoming flow minus outgoing flow at `z` is

    b_z = w_z(m_z-m).

Such a flow exists because `sum_z b_z=0`. Explicitly, removing an edge
`e=(tail,head)` divides the tree into two components; take `F_e` to be the
negative sum of `b_z` on the tail component. When `P` is ordered on the
integer line and the edges point from `z_j` to `z_(j+1)`, this reads

    F_j = sum_(k<=j) w_(z_k)(m-m_(z_k)).                 (1)

For arbitrary real numbers `h_z`, elementary finite summation gives

    sum_z w_z(m_z-m) h_z
      = sum_e F_e(h_head-h_tail).                     (2)

There is no assertion that an edge flow is nonnegative.

Define the integer flux

    J(t) = sum_e F_e(P_head(t)-P_tail(t)).             (3)

Equation (2) shows that the value of `J` is independent of the chosen tree
or of the particular flow with this divergence. Exactly, for EVERY real
`t` and for the specified CLOSED cap,

    integral_(L>=t) (L-m) dmu
       = sum_z kappa_z(t) + J(t).                    (4)

Proof: write `L-m=(L-m_z)+(m_z-m)` separately in each fiber and apply
(2) with `h_z=P_z(t)`. In particular the coefficient of the integer flux
is exactly `1`, not a dimension-dependent constant or an asymptotic loss.

## 2. Integration by parts and the density version

For every continuously differentiable function `phi` on a neighborhood
of the compact scalar support, one has

    integral (L-m) phi(L) dmu
      = integral_R [sum_z kappa_z(t)] phi'(t) dt
        + sum_e F_e [E_head phi(L)-E_tail phi(L)]
      = integral_R [sum_z kappa_z(t)+J(t)] phi'(t) dt. (5)

Here each `E_z` uses the normalized measure `mu_z/w_z`. To prove the
first equality, choose `a` below the scalar support and write
`phi(s)=phi(a)+integral_a^s phi'(t)dt`. The centered constant terms vanish
fiberwise, and Fubini gives the `kappa_z` terms. Applying the same formula
to the difference of two probability laws gives the last equality. All
integrals are over a fixed bounded interval; Fubini is therefore justified
also for atomic or lower-dimensional fiber measures.

In distributional/Stieltjes notation the same identity says

    d kappa_z(t) = (m_z-t) dnu_z(t),
    d J(t) = -sum_z (m_z-m) dnu_z(t),
    d [sum_z kappa_z(t)+J(t)] = (m-t) dnu(t),          (6)

where `nu=sum_z nu_z`. Closed tail functions are left-continuous at their
jumps; their distributional derivatives in (6) include the full atoms.

Now suppose `d>=1`, each `mu_z` is ordinary `d`-volume on a convex body
`K_z`, and `u!=0`. The scalar law has density

    f_z(t) = H_(d-1)(K_z intersect {v.z+u.x=t})/|u|,
    f(t) = sum_z f_z(t).

All the following derivative identities hold almost everywhere:

    P_z'(t) = -f_z(t)/w_z,
    (sum_z kappa_z)'(t) = (m-t)f(t)+R(t),
    J'(t) = -R(t),
    R(t) = sum_z (m_z-m)f_z(t).                       (7)

Where `f(t)>0`, the canonical scalar Stein kernel is

    tau(t) = [sum_z kappa_z(t)+J(t)]/f(t),

and `(tau f)'=(m-t)f` follows from (7). The within-fiber term alone has
the extra signed derivative `R`; the corresponding integrated correction
is exactly `J`. No monotonicity of the conditional integer index or of
the conditional fiber means has been invoked.

When `u=0`, the scalar law is atomic. Equations (1)--(6) remain valid;
the density and coarea notation in (7) is not used.

An optional exact path representation makes the finite-difference nature
of the correction explicit. For any coupling `pi_e` of the normalized
measures of the tail and head fibers, put `s=L(tail,x)` and
`s'=L(head,x')`. Then

    E_head phi(L)-E_tail phi(L)
      = integral dpi_e integral_0^1
          (s'-s) phi'((1-r)s+r s') dr.                (8)

This is the fundamental theorem of calculus, integrated against the
coupling. The coefficient `s'-s` is signed. Interpolated points in (8)
are not being assigned mixed-integer volume or being selected as a center.

## 3. Actual cap displacement and what section stationarity gives

Let `y_*=(z_*,x_*)`, and write a cap through this point as

    v.(z-z_*) + u.(x-x_*) >= 0,  u!=0.

Assume each positive-volume fiber is either cut properly, or lies strictly
on one side of the cap plane. This excludes supporting-facet coincidences
only for the differential statement in this section, not for (1)--(6).
At a proper cut, use coarea and define

    S_z = H_(d-1)(K_z intersect boundary H)/|u|,
    X_z = (1/|u|) integral_(K_z intersect boundary H) x dH_(d-1).

Vary the cap normal by `(delta v,delta u)` and its center inside the
fixed fiber by `delta x=h`. The derivative of its unnormalized mass is

    delta mu(H)
      = delta v . sum_z (z-z_*) S_z
        + delta u . sum_z (X_z-x_* S_z)
        - (u.h) sum_z S_z.                           (9)

This follows fiberwise by integrating the affine normal displacement on
the cutting section. The strict full/empty fibers contribute zero; there
are finitely many fibers. At a cap that locally minimizes mass over its
normal with the center fixed, differentiability consequently gives

    sum_z z S_z = z_* sum_z S_z,
    sum_z X_z = x_* sum_z S_z.                       (10)

Normal rescaling creates no obstruction: the anchored cap is defined on
an open set of nonzero ambient normals, so every small normal variation
can be used; the derivative in its scaling direction is automatically
zero. Equation (10) is the full ambient section-centroid condition.

Crucially, (10) conditions the actual coordinates on the cutting plane.
It does not replace the unconditional fiber mean `m_z` by `m`, and it does
not eliminate either `R` or `J` in (7). The next example realizes this
distinction at a global mixed-depth maximizer.

## 4. An exact trapezoid center

In continuous coordinates `(x,y)`, let

    K_0 = conv{(-1,0),(1,0),(1/2,1),(-1/2,1)}.

At height `y in [0,1]` its horizontal section is
`[-(1-y/2),1-y/2]`. Its area is `V_0=3/2`, and its centroid is
`(0,g_0)` where `g_0=4/9`. Define

    t = (4-sqrt(7))/3,
    Delta = t-4/9 = (8-3sqrt(7))/9 > 0,
    D = 2t-t^2 = (1+2sqrt(7))/9.

We prove that the maximum unnormalized halfspace depth of `K_0` is
exactly `D`, attained at `p=(0,t)`.

For a nonhorizontal line through `p`, consider the right-hand cap

    x >= s(y-t),

and let its area be `A(s)`. Reflection in the vertical axis gives
`A(-s)=V_0-A(s)`, since the cap boundary has area zero. It suffices first
to study `s>=0`. Put `k=1/2` and `s_1=k/(1-t)`.

For `0<=s<=s_1`, the line cuts the top and bottom sides and

    A(s) = V_0/2 - s(1/2-t).

This is decreasing, since `t<1/2`. For `s_1<=s<=1/t`, the cap is a
triangle whose upper height is `(1+st)/(s+k)`, so

    A(s) = (1+st)^2/[2(s+k)].                        (11)

Its derivative has the sign of `st+2kt-1`. Its minimum occurs at

    s_* = 1/t-1,
    A(s_*) = 2t-t^2 = D.

Indeed `s_1<=s_*<=1/t`: the first inequality is equivalent to
`(t-1/2)(t-2)>=0`, and `0<t<1/2`.

For `s>=1/t`, the line cuts both slanted sides, at heights

    y_0=(st-1)/(s-k),   y_1=(st+1)/(s+k).

Differentiating only the partially occupied horizontal slices gives

    A'(s) = -(1/2)[(y_1-t)^2-(y_0-t)^2] > 0,

because `y_1-t=(1-kt)/(s+k)` and
`y_0-t=-(1-kt)/(s-k)`. Thus it increases to the horizontal lower-cap area

    D_bottom = 2t-t^2/2.

The supremum of `A(s)` on finite `s>=0` is `D_bottom`: its other endpoint value
is `V_0/2=3/4`, whereas `t>4/9` implies
`D_bottom>64/81>3/4`. Its minimum is `D`. The defining equation
`3t^2-8t+3=0` gives

    V_0-D_bottom = D.

Reflection now proves that every nonhorizontal cap through `p` has area
at least `D`; the two horizontal caps have the same asserted lower bound.
Any containing cap can be shrunk to pass through `p`, so the point's
depth is at least `D`.

The two caps with inward normals `(1,-s_*)`, `(-1,-s_*)` and the upper
horizontal cap, all through `p`, each have area `D`. These three normals
have the positive dependence

    (1,-s_*) + (-1,-s_*) + 2s_*(0,1) = 0.

Consequently the three CLOSED caps cover the whole plane: a point strictly
outside all three would contradict this dependence. They bound the depth
of every point of `K_0` above by `D`. This proves the claim.

## 5. A mixed convex body with negative flux at its deepest active cap

Set

    c = g_0+Delta/2,   epsilon=Delta/4,
    K_1 = [-epsilon,epsilon] x [c-epsilon,c+epsilon],
    V_1 = 4epsilon^2 = Delta^2/4.

Take the full-dimensional compact convex body in `R x R^2`

    C = conv( {0} x K_0 union {1} x K_1 ).

Its integer projection is exactly `{0,1}`, and its two integer fibers are
exactly `K_0,K_1`. Let `mu` be the sum of their two-dimensional volumes.
For a point in an extreme fiber, every within-fiber halfspace can be
extended to an ambient halfspace excluding the entire other bounded
fiber, by choosing a sufficiently large integer coefficient of the
appropriate sign. Thus its mixed unnormalized depth is exactly its
ordinary unnormalized depth within its own fiber.

It follows from Section 4 that `y_*=(0,0,t)` has mixed depth `D`. Every
point of the second fiber has depth at most `V_1/2`, because a rectangle
has maximum halfspace depth half its area. The latter assertion follows
by central symmetry for the lower bound at its center and by choosing
the smaller of two complementary through-point halfspaces for the upper
bound at every point. The first fiber has maximum `D` by Section 4.
Moreover `Delta<1/18`, hence `V_1/2<1/2592<D`. Therefore `y_*` is an
actual global mixed-depth maximizer; its normalized depth is `D/M`, with
`M=V_0+V_1`.

Consider the ambient cap `H={y>=t}`, with zero integer coefficient.
The whole second fiber is strictly below its boundary because
`c+epsilon=g_0+3Delta/4<t`. Its first-fiber area is `D`, so it is an
actual minimizing cap at `y_*`. The only nonempty cap section is the
horizontal symmetric segment in `K_0`. Its full ambient centroid is
exactly `y_*`, verifying (10) directly. All the differentiability
hypotheses of Section 3 hold at this cap.

Apply the identity with `L=y`. Its scalar fiber means are

    m_0=g_0,   m_1=c=g_0+Delta/2.

For the edge directed from `0` to `1`, equation (1) gives

    F_0 = V_0(m-m_0) = V_0 V_1 Delta/(2M) > 0.

At the active threshold, `P_0(t)=D/V_0` and `P_1(t)=0`. Consequently

    J(t) = -V_1 Delta D/(2M)
         = -Delta^3 D/(8M) < 0.                     (12)

This is an exact algebraic negative value, at an actual global maximizer
and an active cap having full section-centroid stationarity. It is not
merely a numerical or an auxiliary nonstationary example.

The conditional integer mean also fails monotonicity in this example.
Within the interior of the height interval of `K_1`, the conditional
probability of integer index `1` is positive; immediately above its top
it is zero, while the `K_0` slice still has positive length. Thus one
cannot copy the increasing conditional-coordinate means used for signed
exponential sums into this actual convex mixed family.

The demonstrated obstruction has normalized depth well above the OC
target. It rules out eliminating the signed flux solely from cap
stationarity or global center optimality. It does not rule out an
additional inequality that uses an attained minimum over convex bodies,
all active cap circuits, or an actual below-target cap budget.

## 6. Exact verification

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_mixed_stein_active_flux.py` checks the algebraic center equation,
the three active cap values, the derivative critical point, the flow and
flux formula, and rational bounds separating all regimes. Its checks are
exact symbolic/rational arithmetic. The preceding arguments establish
all halfspace and global-optimality claims without numerical evidence.

## 7. One vector flow for an entire finite critical-cap system

The graph can be fixed once for all ambient normals; it need not be
selected separately for each cap. Write `g_z` for the FULL ambient
barycenter of the normalized fiber measure, so its integer component is
exactly `z`, and put `g=(1/M) sum_z w_z g_z`. On the same oriented tree
choose the vector flow `G_e in R^(n+d)` with

    incoming G minus outgoing G at z = w_z(g_z-g).

For any normal `a`, the scalar flow in Section 1 is exactly
`F_e=a.G_e`. Consider finitely many closed caps
`H_j={a_j.w>=b_j}` and arbitrary nonnegative weights `lambda_j`. Write

    P_zj = mu_z(H_j)/w_z,
    kappa_zj = integral_(H_j intersect fiber z) a_j.(w-g_z) dmu_z.

Summing (4), with no interchange of infinite operations, gives

    sum_j lambda_j integral_(H_j) a_j.(w-g) dmu
      = sum_(z,j) lambda_j kappa_zj
        + sum_e G_e . B_e,                            (13)

where the exact joint cap-boundary flux vector is

    B_e = sum_j lambda_j a_j(P_head,j-P_tail,j).       (14)

Every `kappa_zj` is nonnegative. The last sum has no general sign.
Even a normal balance `sum_j lambda_j a_j=0` by itself does not cancel
(14): the coefficients `P_head,j-P_tail,j` depend on the cap. The actual
global-depth counterexample in Section 5 proves this lack of a sign
already for one cap. It also gives an exact balanced-normal example:
add the opposite closed cap `{y<=t}`, with the same weight. Cap boundaries
have zero measure, so its probability differences are the negatives of
those for `{y>=t}`, and its normal is the negative normal. Its flux
therefore equals `J(t)`, and the balanced pair has total flux `2J(t)<0`.
These two caps cover `S`; only the upper one is an active minimum cap,
so this does not purport to refute an equal-budget critical-cover bound.
Equation (13) retains the additional cap/fiber
incidence information which any simultaneous-budget argument would need
to control; it does not assert that an actual critical-cap system has
arbitrary incidence data.

Two subsequent exact results delimit this further. In
`candidate 02ab05d91af31cbf`, equal-budget caps whose
mass is confined to one fiber have nonnegative weighted flux when their
raw continuous normals balance. In
`candidate ae6d727221cffaef`, a three-fiber convex
body has an actual equal-budget active opposite pair with both full
normal and coarea-gradient balance, yet both fluxes are `-7/624`.
Its depth is `1/2`, so an additional below-OC or minimizing-body
hypothesis is still a separate matter.
